title: Business, trade and commerce
subject: Business Studies
summary: Business is an economic activity of producing or exchanging goods and services for profit, supported by trade and the auxiliaries to trade.
points: Human activities are either economic (done to earn a living) or non-economic (done out of love, sympathy or obligation).
Business, profession and employment differ in the nature of work, the reward, the risk and the code of conduct.
Business activities include industry (primary, secondary and tertiary) and commerce.
Commerce covers trade plus the auxiliaries to trade: transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, advertising and packaging.
Business risk arises from uncertainty and is unavoidable, though it can be reduced by insurance and planning.
example: A steel plant (secondary industry) sells through wholesalers and retailers (trade) and uses lorries, bank credit and a warehouse (auxiliaries to trade).
mistakes: Treating a profession as a business because both earn money — a profession needs a code of conduct and specialised qualification.
Forgetting that tertiary industry is a service industry, not a form of trade.

title: Forms of business organisation
subject: Business Studies
summary: Businesses are organised as sole proprietorships, partnership firms, Hindu Undivided Families, cooperative societies or companies, depending on ownership, liability and control.
points: A sole proprietorship is owned by one person, has unlimited liability, no separate legal entity and optional registration.
A partnership is governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932; minimum two partners, and registration is optional but advisable.
A Hindu Undivided Family business is managed by the karta, with coparceners sharing ownership.
A cooperative society is registered under the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 (or state law), needs at least 10 members and follows one member, one vote.
A company has a separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability and a minimum of 2 members in private and 7 in public companies.
example: Two friends starting a shop would choose a partnership for pooled capital, while wanting limited liability pushes them to a private company.
mistakes: Saying partnership registration is compulsory — it is optional, though an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties.
Confusing perpetual succession (continuity of the company) with limited liability.

title: Public, private and global enterprises
subject: Business Studies
summary: The public sector uses departmental undertakings, statutory corporations and government companies, while the private and global sectors work through MNCs, joint ventures and public-private partnerships.
points: A departmental undertaking is a business arm of a ministry, controlled by government rules and funded through the budget.
A statutory corporation is created by a special Act, which sets its objects, powers and duties.
A government company has at least 51 per cent of paid-up capital held by government.
A multinational corporation operates in more than one country through subsidiaries, branches or joint ventures.
Public-private partnership and joint ventures combine public accountability with private efficiency.
example: Indian Railways is a departmental undertaking, while a government company has at least 51 per cent government-held paid-up capital.
mistakes: Thinking any company funded by government is a statutory corporation — it must be created by an Act.
Mixing a holding company's subsidiaries with MNC branches.

title: Emerging modes of business: e-business and outsourcing
subject: Business Studies
summary: E-business conducts business over electronic networks, and outsourcing moves selected activities to outside specialists.
points: E-business covers B2B, B2C, C2C and intra-B transactions.
An online transaction has three stages: registration, placing the order and payment.
Payment can be cash on delivery, cheque, net banking, card or a digital wallet and UPI.
E-business gives speed, reach and convenience but raises security, privacy and delivery risks.
Outsourcing includes BPO, KPO and legal process outsourcing, and is used for non-core activities.
example: A student buying shoes from a shopping website is a B2C transaction; the same retailer buying stock from a factory online is B2B.
mistakes: Calling every online activity an e-business — it must be a commercial transaction.
Confusing BPO (routine processes) with KPO (knowledge-intensive work).

title: Social responsibility of business and business ethics
subject: Business Studies
summary: Businesses owe duties to owners, workers, consumers, government and the public, and CSR is now partly a legal obligation in India.
points: Business responsibilities are economic, legal, ethical and discretionary.
CSR under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 applies to companies crossing specified net worth, turnover or net profit thresholds.
Such companies must spend at least 2 per cent of average net profits of the preceding three years on CSR.
Business ethics covers honest advertising, fair dealing with employees and truthful disclosure.
Environmental protection includes pollution control, waste recycling and conserving natural resources.

formulas.name: CSR spending
formulas.expr: CSR = 2% × average net profit of the last 3 years

example: A listed company that meets the Section 135 thresholds must spend 2 per cent of its three-year average net profit on CSR activities.
mistakes: Treating CSR as charity — it is a structured responsibility towards stakeholders.
Calling legal compliance itself CSR — obeying the law is the legal, not the discretionary, level.

title: Nature and significance of management
subject: Business Studies
summary: Management is the process of getting things done through others to achieve goals efficiently and effectively.
points: Management is goal-oriented, all-pervasive, multidimensional and continuous.
It is an art, a science and a profession at the same time.
The three levels are top, middle and supervisory management.
The functions are planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.
Coordination is the essence of management and runs through every function.
example: A factory manager who plans output, assigns work and checks results is performing all five functions of management.
mistakes: Treating management as a single activity rather than a process.
Assuming coordination is a separate sixth function — it is the essence threading through the rest.

title: Internal trade
subject: Business Studies
summary: Internal trade is buying and selling within a country, through wholesale and retail trade.
points: Wholesalers buy in bulk from producers and sell in smaller lots to retailers.
Retailers sell to final consumers through itinerant or fixed-shop forms.
Departmental stores offer many product lines under one roof, while chain stores have similar lines across branches.
Mail order, tele-shopping and online retailing are non-store retail formats.
Goods and Services Tax has replaced most indirect taxes on internal trade.
example: A wholesaler buys 1,000 sacks of rice from a mill and supplies 50 sacks each to nearby retail shops.
mistakes: Calling internal trade foreign trade — the buyer and seller are in the same country.
Confusing a departmental store (many lines) with a chain store (similar line, many branches).

title: International business
subject: Business Studies
summary: International business crosses national borders and differs from domestic trade in currency, law, documentation and risk.
points: International business includes imports, exports, licensing, franchising and foreign direct investment.
Export and import procedures involve documents such as the invoice, bill of lading, shipping bill and letter of credit.
Export promotion measures include SEZs, export-oriented units and incentives.
International business faces higher political, currency and documentation risk than domestic trade.
The World Trade Organization frames rules for international trade.
example: An Indian firm exporting garments is paid through a letter of credit arranged by the buyer's bank, reducing payment risk.
mistakes: Assuming international business is only export — imports, licensing and FDI also count.
Mixing a bill of lading (shipment document) with an invoice (demand for payment).

title: Theory base of accounting
subject: Accountancy
summary: Accounting follows generally accepted principles built on basic assumptions, concepts and conventions.
points: The basic assumptions are going concern, consistency and accrual.
Key principles include accounting entity, money measurement, matching, dual aspect, revenue recognition and full disclosure.
Conventions include conservatism, materiality and consistency.
The dual aspect principle gives the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus capital.
GST is split into CGST, SGST and IGST, and input tax credit avoids taxing the same value twice.
example: Recording a sale only when goods are delivered follows the revenue recognition principle.
mistakes: Applying conservatism to create hidden reserves — it allows provision for losses, not deliberate understatement.
Treating the going concern assumption as a rule for closing the business.

title: Recording of transactions
subject: Accountancy
summary: Transactions are supported by source documents, recorded in vouchers and the journal, then posted to ledger accounts.
points: Source documents include invoices, receipts, debit and credit notes, pay-in-slips and cheques.
A voucher is prepared from the source document before entry is made.
Debit the receiver and credit the giver is the traditional rule; modern rules use increases and decreases in assets, liabilities, capital, revenue and expenses.
A compound journal entry records more than two accounts in one entry.
GST paid on purchases is debited to input CGST, SGST or IGST, and GST collected on sales is credited to output accounts.
example: Goods bought for cash: purchases account is debited and cash account is credited.
mistakes: Debiting an increase in capital — capital increases on the credit side.
Posting the same amount twice in the ledger after a compound entry.

title: Accounts from incomplete records
subject: Accountancy
summary: When books are incomplete, profit is found by comparing opening and closing capital after adjusting drawings and fresh capital.
points: Incomplete records mean some transactions are not recorded, so a trial balance cannot be prepared.
The statement of affairs method lists assets and liabilities to find capital at two dates.
Profit equals closing capital plus drawings minus additional capital minus opening capital.
Missing figures such as credit sales or cash purchases are found with total debtors and creditors accounts.
This method is an estimate, so it is less reliable than a full double-entry system.

formulas.name: Profit from capital comparison
formulas.expr: Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital

example: Opening capital ₹50,000, closing capital ₹70,000, drawings ₹5,000 and no fresh capital gives a profit of ₹25,000.
mistakes: Forgetting to add drawings back before computing profit.
Treating the statement of affairs as a balance sheet prepared under double entry.

title: Computerised accounting system
subject: Accountancy
summary: A computerised accounting system records and reports transactions through accounting software built on a database.
points: Its components are hardware, software, people, procedures and data.
Accounting software may be ready-to-use, customised or tailor-made.
Advantages include speed, accuracy, reliability, legibility and instant management reports.
Limitations include cost of installation and training, data security risk and dependence on the system.
The accounting framework, coding structure and security policy must be designed before data entry begins.
example: A trader using tally-type software enters a voucher once and the ledger, trial balance and GST returns update automatically.
mistakes: Believing software removes the need for accounting knowledge — the principles still decide the entries.
Ignoring backups, which leaves data vulnerable to system failure.

title: Accounting ratios
subject: Accountancy
summary: Ratios express the relationship between two accounting figures and measure liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability.
points: Liquidity ratios include the current ratio and the quick ratio.
Solvency ratios include debt-equity and proprietary ratios.
Activity ratios include inventory turnover, trade receivables turnover and working capital turnover.
Profitability ratios include gross profit, net profit and return on investment.
A ratio is meaningful only when compared with past years, another firm or an industry standard.

formulas.name: Quick ratio
formulas.expr: (current assets − inventory − prepaid expenses) ÷ current liabilities

formulas.name: Inventory turnover
formulas.expr: cost of revenue from operations ÷ average inventory

formulas.name: Return on investment
formulas.expr: (net profit before interest, tax and dividend ÷ capital employed) × 100

example: Current assets ₹3,00,000 and current liabilities ₹1,50,000 give a current ratio of 2:1, which is generally considered satisfactory.
mistakes: Using closing inventory instead of average inventory in turnover ratios.
Comparing a ratio across firms of very different size or industry without adjustment.

title: Dissolution of partnership firm
subject: Accountancy
summary: Dissolution ends the partnership firm itself, and its assets and liabilities are settled through a realisation account.
points: Dissolution of partnership changes the relation between partners; dissolution of the firm ends the firm.
Modes include dissolution by agreement, compulsory dissolution, on insolvency, on expiry or on completion of the venture.
A realisation account records the sale of assets, payment of liabilities and realisation expenses.
Assets and liabilities are transferred to the realisation account at book value, and the profit or loss is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Under the Garner v Murray rule, a deficient partner's capital shortfall is borne by solvent partners in the ratio of their capitals.

formulas.name: Realisation profit
formulas.expr: realisation profit = assets realised + liabilities taken over − assets book value − liabilities paid − expenses

example: Assets of book value ₹2,00,000 realise ₹1,70,000, giving a realisation loss of ₹30,000 shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
mistakes: Crediting the realisation account with the book value of assets instead of the amount realised.
Paying partners' capitals before outside liabilities and partners' loans.

title: Financial statements of a company
subject: Accountancy
summary: A company presents its balance sheet and statement of profit and loss in the Schedule III format, and analyses them with comparative and common-size statements.
points: The balance sheet is prepared in the prescribed Schedule III form with equity and liabilities, and assets.
The statement of profit and loss shows revenue, other income, expenses, tax and profit after tax.
Comparative statements show figures for two or more years side by side with absolute and percentage change.
A common-size statement expresses each item as a percentage of total revenue or total assets.
Notes to accounts and significant accounting policies form part of the statements.
example: If revenue rises from ₹5,00,000 to ₹6,00,000, the percentage change is 20 per cent.
mistakes: Computing a percentage change with the current year as the denominator.
Comparing a common-size percentage of revenue with one of total assets.
aliases: statement of profit and loss company

title: Collection and organisation of data
subject: Economics
summary: Economic statistics begin with collecting data from primary or secondary sources and organising it into a frequency distribution.
points: Primary data are collected first-hand; secondary data are already published.
Primary methods include direct personal investigation, indirect oral investigation and questionnaires.
A census covers every unit; a sample covers a selected part of the population.
Sampling methods include random, stratified, systematic, multistage and quota sampling.
Organised data use tally marks, class intervals, class limits, mid-values and frequency distributions.
example: Marks grouped as 40–50, 50–60 and 60–70 have a class width of 10 and mid-values 45, 55 and 65.
mistakes: Calling published census tables primary data.
Leaving overlapping class limits, so a value such as 50 could fall in two classes.

title: Correlation and index numbers
subject: Economics
summary: Correlation measures how closely two variables move together, and index numbers express change over time relative to a base period.
points: Correlation can be positive or negative, linear or non-linear, simple or multiple.
Karl Pearson's coefficient lies between −1 and +1, and zero means no linear relation.
Spearman's rank correlation suits qualitative data that can be ranked.
A simple index number compares a current value with a base-year value, usually multiplied by 100.
Index numbers are used for inflation, production and the cost of living, but they are only as good as their base and weights.
example: If the price of a good rises from ₹40 in the base year to ₹50 now, the index number is 125.
mistakes: Reading a high correlation as proof of causation.
Ignoring the base year when comparing two index numbers.

title: Infrastructure
subject: Economics
summary: Infrastructure covers the economic and social services on which production and welfare depend, such as energy, transport, education and health.
points: Economic infrastructure includes energy, transport and communication.
Social infrastructure includes education, health and housing.
Infrastructure is a public good with long gestation periods and large indivisible investment.
India depends heavily on coal and oil but is expanding solar, wind and hydro capacity.
Health and education spending shape human capital and long-run growth.
example: A power plant that takes ten years to build illustrates the long gestation and lumpy investment of infrastructure.
mistakes: Treating schools and hospitals as economic infrastructure — they are social infrastructure.
Assuming infrastructure is only physical transport.

title: Environment and sustainable development
subject: Economics
summary: Development that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs is sustainable development.
points: Natural resources are renewable or non-renewable, and both can be depleted or degraded.
Pollution of air, water, soil and noise imposes health and economic costs.
Sustainable development needs population control, efficient resource use, renewable energy and pollution abatement.
Movements such as Chipko and struggles over forests and dams shaped Indian environmental policy.
Global warming, ozone depletion and biodiversity loss need international cooperation.
example: Using harvested rainwater and solar pumps on a farm cuts groundwater use and emissions at the same time.
mistakes: Equating sustainable development with stopping growth altogether.
Calling a resource renewable while using it faster than it regenerates.
